children.translated_text: Therefore, it is the universal form (<s>ākṛti</s>) alone that is denoted [by words].
If the action of threshing and the like does not culminate in the universal form, then the individual should be indicated there [by the universal].

Moreover, in passages such as '<s>śyonarcittaṃ cinvīta</s>' (one should construct [the fire-altar] in the shape of a hawk), the connection with the action is seen through the universal form alone, by way of its being the correlate of similarity.
Therefore, the universal form (<s>ākṛti</s>) is the meaning of words. || MJaiNyC_1,2.33-34 ||

In usages such as '<s>vrīhīn avahanti</s>' (they thresh rice), '<s>paśum ālabheta</s>' (one should sacrifice an animal), '<s>gām ānaya</s>' (bring a cow), '<s>brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ</s>' (a Brahmin should not be killed), and so on, the meaning of words like '<s>vrīhi</s>' and the like is the particular individual (<s>vyakti</s>). Why? Because the individual is capable of being connected with actions such as threshing and the like. For the universal form (<s>ākṛti</s>) is not fit to be threshed, sacrificed, or brought. But if it be argued that etymological derivation (<s>vyutpatti</s>) is not possible in the individual due to infinity and deviation — for the individuals are infinite, since the number of cows past, future, and present in many places cannot be determined; moreover, the word '<s>go</s>' (cow), when learned with reference to a white individual, would deviate from its [established] meaning when applied to a black individual — how then is derivation possible? If so, then at the time of derivation, let the individual be indicated by the universal form — having arrived at this position, we say: Since the apprehension of [word-meaning] capacity (<s>śaktigrahaṇa</s>) through agreement (<s>anvaya</s>) and difference (<s>vyatireka</s>) is based on the universal form (<s>ākṛti</s>), it is appropriate that the universal form alone is the meaning of words. Moreover, for one who holds the individual view, there would be doubt when the word '<s>go</s>' is uttered [as to which individual is meant].
START MJaiNy 1,3.35
On this very topic, he states the teacher's view —
Let the Vedic injunction regarding '<s>go</s>' (cow) and the like not be [compromised] by the non-determination between the universal (<s>jāti</s>) and the individual (<s>vyakti</s>);
the conclusion is that it is not the individual, due to infinity and deviation. // MJaiNy_1,3.35 //
The meaning is clear. || MJaiNyC_1,2.35 ||

children.translated_text: no.
Because it is included in the injunctive portion as the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>).

children.text: yadyapi liṅpratyayena samānapadopātto yajidhātvarthaḥ karaṇam tathāpi tasya yajernāmatvenodbhidādipadamanveti |
children.translated_text: Although the meaning of the root '<s>yaj</s>' (to sacrifice), which is taken up in the same word [as the injunctive suffix] through the <s>liṅ</s> suffix, is the instrument, nevertheless the word '<s>Udbhid</s>' and the like is connected with it as the name of that sacrifice.
Therefore it is a means of knowledge. || MJaiNyC_1,4.1-2 ||

It is handed down thus: '<s>udbhidā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Udbhid</s>), '<s>balabhidā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Balabhid</s>), '<s>viśvajitā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Viśvajit</s>). Therein, the word '<s>Udbhid</s>' and the like is not a means of knowledge regarding <s>dharma</s>. Why? Because it cannot be included in the three divisions of the Veda that are accepted as authoritative. Namely: injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) is directly a means of knowledge; laudatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>) and <s>mantra</s> are [means of knowledge] through their connection with injunction. Now, the word '<s>Udbhid</s>' and the like is not included in the injunctive portion — because it does not express any of the components of <s>bhāvanā</s> (the productive force), which is the meaning of the injunction, namely the object to be produced (<s>bhāvya</s>), the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>), or the mode of procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>). Nor is it a laudatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>), because there is no cognition of praise. Nor is it a <s>mantra</s>, because the indicators of a <s>mantra</s> — first person [address], invocation, and the like — are absent. As it has been said: 'Due to the absence of first person, invocation, end-markers, internal form, and the like, and because there is no established convention of <s>mantra</s>-hood, <s>mantra</s>-status for these [words] is not appropriate.' '<s>agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi</s>' (I offer what is pleasing to <s>Agni</s>) — this is first person. '<s>agne yaśasvin yaśase samarpaya</s>' (O glorious <s>Agni</s>, bestow upon glory) — this is invocation. '<s>urvī cāsi vasvī cāsi</s>' (you are wide, you are wealthy) — this is internal form. '<s>iṣe tvā ūrje tvā</s>' (for nourishment, for vigor) — this is the '<s>tvā</s>'-ending form. The word 'and the like' [includes] blessings, identification of the deity, and so on. If it be argued that since it cannot be included in [any of] these [categories], it is not a means of knowledge —
START MJaiNy 1,4.3-4
(In the second <s>adhikaraṇa</s>, on the status of words like '<s>Udbhid</s>' as names of sacrifices, the <s>sūtra</s> is:)

children.text: api vā nāmadheyaṃ syād yad utpattāv apūrvam avidhāyakatvāt / Jaim_1,4.2 /
children.translated_text: Or rather, it would be a name, since it is unprecedented at the time of origination and is non-injunctive. / Jaim_1,4.2 /
He composes the second <s>adhikaraṇa</s> —
Is this [word '<s>Udbhid</s>'] a qualifying attribute (<s>guṇa</s>) or a name (<s>nāmadheya</s>)? From its etymology, it [denotes] a spade (<s>khanitra</s>);
with reference to the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> [sacrifice], it would be an injunction of a qualifying attribute for the purpose of [obtaining] cattle. // MJaiNy_1,4.3 //
Since the etymological derivation is the same because of the breaking forth of fruit, it applies to the sacrifice-name as well;
name-status is appropriate, due to co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with the sacrifice. // MJaiNy_1,4.4 //

children.translated_text: The purpose of the name everywhere is simply practical designation (<s>vyavahāra</s>).

children.text: na hyantareṇa nāmadheyamṛtvigvaraṇādiṣu ' anenāhaṃ yakṣye ' ityākhyānopāyo laghuḥ kaścidasti |
children.translated_text: For without a name, there is no easy means of declaration in the selection of priests (<s>ṛtvigvaraṇa</s>) and the like — such as 'I shall sacrifice with this [sacrifice].'
Therefore —
the word '<s>Udbhid</s>' and the like is a name (<s>nāmadheya</s>). || MJaiNyC_1,4.3-4 ||

In '<s>udbhidā yajeta paśukāmaḥ</s>' (one who desires cattle should sacrifice with the <s>Udbhid</s>), the meaning intended by the word '<s>udbhid</s>' in the instrumental case would be some qualifying attribute (<s>guṇa</s>) of the sacrifice — because it is similar to the qualifying-attribute injunction '<s>daghnā juhoti</s>' (one offers with curds). If it be objected that 'the meaning of the word <s>dadhi</s> (curds) is well-known in the world, but the meaning of the word <s>udbhid</s> is not well-known' — that is not so. Because even in the absence of conventional usage (<s>rūḍhi</s>), its meaning is well-known through etymology based on the component meanings: 'that by which the earth is broken up' (<s>udbhidyate bhūmir anena</s>) — by this derivation, the word denotes a spade (<s>khanitra</s>). Nor should it be said that no sacrifice with the fruit of cattle is being enjoined here — because cattle are the fruit of the qualifying attribute. Just as in '<s>godohanena paśukāmasya</s>' (for one desiring cattle, [the offering is performed] with the milking of a cow), the cattle are the fruit of the qualifying attribute of cow-milking, so here too let them be the fruit of the qualifying attribute of the spade. If the cow-milking is enjoined with reference to the established primary rite of water-carrying prescribed by '<s>camasenāpaḥ praṇayet</s>' (one should carry water with a ladle), then here too let the spade be enjoined with reference to the established primary rite of the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> sacrifice prescribed by '<s>jyotiṣṭomena yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>). Therefore it is a qualifying-attribute injunction — having arrived at this position, we say: The meaning of the two words '<s>paśukāmo yajeta</s>' (one who desires cattle should sacrifice) is 'one should produce the fruit in the form of cattle through a sacrifice.' When the expectation arises 'by which sacrifice?' — the word '<s>udbhidā</s>' in the instrumental case is connected as the name of the sacrifice. The name-status of the word '<s>udbhid</s>' is established by the etymology: 'by this sacrifice the fruit of cattle breaks forth' (<s>udbhidyate paśuphalam anena yāgena</s>). If it be argued that since the etymological analysis is equally applicable to both the qualifying-attribute injunction and name-status, there is no determination — that is not correct. Because co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) is the deciding factor. When it is said 'one should produce the fruit through a sacrifice named <s>Udbhid</s>,' co-referentiality is obtained. But if it were a qualifying attribute, there would be non-co-referentiality (<s>vaiyadhikaraṇya</s>) — 'by a sacrifice accomplished with a spade.' If one tried to construe co-referentiality as 'by a sacrifice possessing a spade,' then a secondary usage of the possessive type (<s>matvarthalakṣaṇā</s>) would be required. Therefore the word '<s>Udbhid</s>' and the like is a name. In cases like '<s>dadhnā juhoti</s>' (one offers with curds) and '<s>vrīhibhir yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with rice), since the words <s>dadhi</s> and the like have extremely well-established conventional meanings denoting specific substances, name-status for sacrifices is impossible, and so qualifying-attribute status is necessarily resorted to. In '<s>somena yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with <s>Soma</s>) as well, with the reasoning that 'it is better to resort to secondary usage through the well-known meaning than to postulate name-status with an unknown meaning,' the possessive secondary usage '<s>somadravyavatā yāgena</s>' (by a sacrifice possessing the substance <s>Soma</s>) was accepted. But since the word '<s>udbhid</s>' has no well-known worldly meaning, name-status in the manner described is appropriate.
START MJaiNy 1,4.5
On this very topic, he states the teacher's view —
If [it be objected that] this injunction, in the case of a worldly communal sacrifice (<s>gaṇayāga</s>), requires [an external basis] —
due to name-status of the Vedic sacrifice established by etymology, there is no such dependence. // MJaiNy_1,4.5 //
And no Vedic (<s>śrauta</s>) basis is found for it.
Therefore, a worldly sacrifice such as the <s>mātṛgaṇayāga</s> (communal sacrifice to the divine mothers) and the like should be accepted as its basis.
Against that view [we say]: that is not correct.
Because when the name-status of the Vedic sacrifice is established by the etymology described above, there is no dependence [on an external basis]. || MJaiNyC_1,4.5 ||
'<s>Udbhidā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Udbhid</s>) — this is a qualifying-attribute injunction.
START MJaiNy 1,4.6-7
(In the third <s>adhikaraṇa</s>, on the status of words like '<s>Citrā</s>' as names of sacrifices, the <s>sūtra</s> is:)
That in which there is instruction of a qualifying attribute, its connection is with the principal [sacrifice]. / Jaim_1,4.3 /
He composes the third <s>adhikaraṇa</s> —

children.text: yaccitrayā yajeteti tadguṇo nāma vā bhavet /
children.translated_text: In '<s>citrayā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Citrā</s>), is this [word] a qualifying attribute or a name?
The word '<s>citrā</s>' is a qualifying attribute [meaning 'variegated'] — [the animal] being variegated, by conventional usage, in the <s>Agnīṣomīya</s> animal [sacrifice]. // MJaiNy_1,4.6 //
If both [qualify as] an injunction, there would be a splitting of the sentence; and there is the burden [of postulating] a special [connection] — therefore,
let it be a name; and the same applies in the <s>Pṛṣṭhya</s>, <s>Ājya</s>, and <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> [rites]. // MJaiNy_1,4.7 //

children.translated_text: If the words '<s>bahiṣpavamāna</s>,' '<s>ājya</s>,' and '<s>pṛṣṭha</s>' were also enjoiners of qualifying attributes, then [these sentences] would serve as counter-examples [to the established rule].
The enjoining of two qualifying attributes [in one sentence] would cause a splitting of the sentence.
Therefore, the words '<s>bahiṣpavamāna</s>' and the like are names of <s>stotras</s> (chants).
Through those names, the rites are restated, and the qualifying attributes such as <s>Trivṛt</s> and the like are enjoined. || MJaiNyC_1,4.6-7 ||

It is handed down: '<s>citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ</s>' (one who desires cattle should sacrifice with the <s>Citrā</s>). Therein, the word '<s>citrā</s>' is not etymological (<s>yaugika</s>) like the word '<s>udbhid</s>,' but rather, by conventional usage (<s>rūḍhi</s>), it denotes variegatedness and femininity. Therefore, name-status does not follow by the previous reasoning. This being so, the entire animal sacrifice prescribed by '<s>agnīṣomīyaṃ paśum ālabheta</s>' (one should sacrifice the <s>Agnīṣomīya</s> animal) is restated by the word '<s>yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice), and in that animal, the two qualifying attributes of variegatedness and femininity are enjoined — having arrived at this position, we say: Variegatedness and femininity — these are two qualifying attributes. If both were enjoined, the sentence would be split. As it has been said: 'When the rite is already established [by another injunction], multiple qualifying attributes cannot be enjoined [by a single sentence]; but when the rite is not yet established, even many [attributes] can be enjoined with a single effort.' Now, if to avoid splitting the sentence, a substance in the form of an animal qualified by both variegatedness and femininity is enjoined as the instrument, then there would be the burden [of undue complexity]. Therefore, the word '<s>citrā</s>' — like the previous cases — becomes a sacrifice-name through co-referentiality with [the verb meaning] sacrifice. The variegatedness is accounted for through the distinctive substances [used in the rite]. '<s>Dadhi</s> (curds), <s>madhu</s> (honey), <s>ghṛta</s> (ghee), <s>āpaḥ</s> (water), <s>dhānāḥ</s> (parched grain), <s>taṇḍulāḥ</s> (husked rice) — the mixture of these is the <s>Prājāpatya</s> [offering]' — thus six variegated offering-substances beginning with curds are handed down. This is the origination-sentence (<s>utpattivākya</s>) of the sacrifice named <s>Citrā</s> — because the offering substances beginning with curds and the deity <s>Prajāpati</s>, which constitute the essential nature of the sacrifice, are taught therein. For the sacrifice thus originated, '<s>citrayā yajeta paśukāmaḥ</s>' (one who desires cattle should sacrifice with the <s>Citrā</s>) — this is the fruit-sentence (<s>phalavākya</s>). When this is the case, the intended meaning is obtained. If a qualifying-attribute injunction were postulated through the restatement of the <s>Agnīṣomīya</s> animal [sacrifice], the faults of abandoning the intended topic and introducing an unintended one would arise. Because accepting the <s>liṅ</s> suffix as restating [a previously enjoined act], the primary injunctive meaning would be overridden. Therefore the word '<s>citrā</s>' is a name. Just as name-status applies to the word '<s>citrā</s>,' so too name-status should be construed for the words '<s>bahiṣpavamāna</s>,' '<s>ājya</s>,' and '<s>pṛṣṭha</s>.' For thus it is heard: '<s>trivṛd bahiṣpavamānam</s>' (the <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> [has the] <s>Trivṛt</s> [stoma]), '<s>pañcadaśāny ājyāni</s>' (the <s>Ājya</s> [stotras have the] fifteen-fold [stoma]), '<s>saptadaśāni pṛṣṭhāni</s>' (the <s>Pṛṣṭha</s> [stotras have the] seventeen-fold [stoma]). The meaning of this triad of sentences is explained [as follows]: In the latter book (<s>uttarāgrantha</s>) [of the Sāmaveda], three-verse hymns (<s>sūktas</s>) are handed down. Among them, '<s>upāsmai gāyata naraḥ</s>' (sing unto him, O men) is the first hymn; '<s>davidyutatyā rucā</s>' (with that flashing radiance) is the second; '<s>pāvamānasya te kave</s>' (of the purifying [Soma], O wise one) is the third. In the performance of the morning pressing (<s>prātaḥsavana</s>) of the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>, the <s>Gāyatra Sāman</s> is to be chanted upon these three hymns. This chant (<s>stotra</s>) accomplished through the singing of the three hymns is called <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> — because the verses therein pertain to <s>Pavamāna</s> (the purifying [Soma]), and because of its external (<s>bahiḥ</s>) connection — for this <s>stotra</s> is not performed inside the sacrificial hall (<s>sadas</s>) near the <s>Audumbarī</s> post like the other <s>stotras</s>, but is performed by those who crawl outside the <s>sadas</s>. The <s>stoma</s> (mode of chanting) of this <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> is the one called <s>Trivṛt</s> (nine-fold). The scriptural sentence prescribing this <s>stoma</s> is handed down thus: '<s>tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa prathamayā, tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa madhyamayā, tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa uttamayā; uhyatī trivṛto viṣṭutiḥ</s>' (he chants '<s>hiṃ</s>' with three, that being with the first [verse of each hymn]; he chants '<s>hiṃ</s>' with three, that being with the middle; he chants '<s>hiṃ</s>' with three, that being with the last; this is the <s>uhyatī viṣṭuti</s> of the <s>Trivṛt</s>). The meaning is: the chanting of the nine verses from the three hymns is to be done in three rounds (<s>paryāya</s>). In the first round, the first verses of the three hymns [are chanted]; in the second round, the middle [verses]; in the third round, the last [verses]. '<s>Tisṛbhyaḥ</s>' — the ablative is used in the sense of the instrumental. '<s>Hiṃ karoti</s>' means 'he chants.' This mode of singing, possessing the described pattern, is the <s>viṣṭuti</s> (specific mode of praise) of the <s>Trivṛt</s> stoma, and it is named <s>uhyatī</s>. Similarly, there are two [other] <s>viṣṭutis</s>: <s>parivartinī</s> and <s>kulāyinī</s>. Of these, <s>parivartinī</s> is handed down thus: '<s>tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa parācībhiḥ, tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa parācībhiḥ, tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa parācībhiḥ; parivartinī trivṛto viṣṭutiḥ</s>' (he chants '<s>hiṃ</s>' with three, that being with those in reverse order; ... this is the <s>parivartinī viṣṭuti</s> of the <s>Trivṛt</s>). '<s>Parācībhiḥ</s>' means 'with those recited in reverse order.' <s>Kulāyinī</s> is handed down thus: '<s>tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti sa parācībhiḥ, tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti — yā madhyamā sā prathamā, yottamā sā madhyamā, yā prathamā sottamā; tisṛbhyo hiṃ karoti — yottamā sā prathamā, yā prathamā sā madhyamā, yā madhyamā sottamā; kulāyinī trivṛto viṣṭutiḥ</s>.' Here, in the first hymn the reading order itself [is followed]; in the second, [the order is] middle, last, first; in the third, last, first, middle — thus the mantras are to be chanted with transposition. This triad of <s>viṣṭutis</s> is offered as alternatives. The meaning of the word '<s>trivṛt</s>' is this form of <s>stoma</s>, not the three <s>guṇas</s> — this was determined in the earlier <s>pāda</s>. In the latter book, above the three <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> hymns, four [more] hymns are handed down: '<s>agna ā yāhi vītaye</s>' (O <s>Agni</s>, come for enjoyment) is the first; '<s>ā no mitrāvaruṇā</s>' (come to us, O <s>Mitra</s> and <s>Varuṇa</s>) is the second; '<s>ā yāhi suṣumā hi te</s>' (come, for your [Soma] is well-pressed) is the third; '<s>indrāgnī ā gataṃ sutam</s>' (O <s>Indra</s> and <s>Agni</s>, come to the pressed [Soma]) is the fourth. These four, sung with the <s>Gāyatra Sāman</s> in the morning pressing, are called the four <s>Ājya</s> stotras. And their etymology is heard: '<s>yad ājam īyuḥ, tad ājyānām ājyatvam</s>' (because they proceeded to the contest, that is the <s>ājya</s>-nature of the <s>ājyas</s>). In these <s>Ājya</s> stotras, the <s>stoma</s> is the one called <s>Pañcadaśa</s> (fifteen-fold). The <s>viṣṭuti</s> of this <s>stoma</s> is handed down thus: '<s>pañcabhyo hiṃ karoti sa tisṛbhiḥ sa ekayā sa ekayā, pañcabhyo hiṃ karoti sa ekayā sa tisṛbhiḥ sa ekayā, pañcabhyo hiṃ karoti sa ekayā sa ekayā sa tisṛbhiḥ</s>' (he chants '<s>hiṃ</s>' with five — three times [with one verse], once [each with the other two]; ...). One hymn is to be repeated three times. In the first repetition, the first verse is chanted three times; in the second, the middle verse; in the third, the last verse. This is the fifteen-fold <s>stoma</s>. Above the four [<s>Ājya</s>] hymns in the latter book, three midday <s>Pavamāna</s> hymns are handed down, and above those, four [more] hymns are handed down. Among these, '<s>abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ</s>' (we praise you, O hero) is the first; '<s>kayā naś citrā ā bhuvat</s>' (with what wondrous [aid] will he come to us?) is the second; '<s>taṃ vo dasmam ṛtīṣaham</s>' (him, the wonder-working, the vanquisher of seasons) is the third; '<s>taro bhir vo vidadvasum</s>' (through powers, finding wealth for you) is the fourth. These, sung in sequence with the <s>Rathantara</s>, <s>Vāmadevya</s>, <s>Naudhasa</s>, and <s>Kāleya</s> Sāmans in the midday pressing, are called the <s>Pṛṣṭha</s> stotras. The etymology '<s>sparśanāt pṛṣṭhāni</s>' (they are <s>pṛṣṭha</s> because of touching) should be understood. In these stotras, the <s>stoma</s> is the seventeen-fold (<s>Saptadaśa</s>). The <s>viṣṭuti</s> of this <s>stoma</s> is handed down thus: '<s>pañcabhyo hiṃ karoti sa tisṛbhiḥ sa ekayā sa ekayā, pañcabhyo hiṃ karoti sa ekayā sa tisṛbhiḥ sa ekayā sa ekayā, pañcabhyo hiṃ karoti sa ekayā sa tisṛbhiḥ sa ekayā, saptabhyo hiṃ karoti sa ekayā sa tisṛbhiḥ sa tisṛbhiḥ</s>.' Here, in the first repetition the first verse is chanted three times; in the second, the middle verse; in the third, both the middle and the last [are repeated]. This is the seventeen-fold <s>stoma</s>. In all three sentences, the words '<s>trivṛt</s>,' '<s>pañcadaśa</s>,' and '<s>saptadaśa</s>' are accepted as enjoining qualifying attributes.
START MJaiNy 1,4.8-12
(In the fourth <s>adhikaraṇa</s>, on the status of words like '<s>Agnihotra</s>' as sacrifice-names — the <s>matprakhya</s> [self-evident name] principle — the <s>sūtra</s> is:)
And [this principle applies to] another <s>śāstra</s> which is designated by that [name]. / Jaim_1,4.4 /

'<s>Agnihotraṃ juhoti</s>' (one offers the <s>Agnihotra</s>) and '<s>āghāram āghārayati</s>' (one pours the <s>āghāra</s>) — are these two
enjoining a qualifying attribute and a preparatory rite (<s>saṃskāra</s>), or are they names of rites? // MJaiNy_1,4.8 //
'<s>Agnaye hotram atra</s>' (the oblation to <s>Agni</s> is here) — [in this reading,] <s>Agni</s> is understood through the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound

children.translated_text: Because after performance, the [ritual] has the appearance of being accomplished, and even in its instrumentality, prior to that [completion], the accusative case is appropriate to express its status as the object to be accomplished — [saying] '<s>agnihotram</s>' and '<s>āghāram</s>' [in the accusative].

children.text: na cātra dvitīyānusāreṇa 'vrīhīnprokṣati ' itrayadāvidya saṃskāraḥ śaṅkanīyaḥ |
children.translated_text: Nor should a preparatory rite (<s>saṃskāra</s>) be suspected here following the accusative case, as in '<s>vrīhīn prokṣati</s>' (one sprinkles the rice).

Because, unlike the word '<s>vrīhi</s>' (rice), the words '<s>agnihotra</s>' and '<s>āghāra</s>' do not have well-established meanings denoting specific substances, and are accepted as denoting actions.

children.text: tasmāt - agnihotrāghāraśabdau darvihomopāṃśuyājayorguṇasaṃskāravidhāyinau na bhavataḥ, kintu karmāntarayornāmanī || MJaiNyC_1,4.8-12 ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, the words '<s>agnihotra</s>' and '<s>āghāra</s>' are not enjoiners of a qualifying attribute and a preparatory rite for the <s>darvihoma</s> and <s>upāṃśuyāja</s> respectively, but rather are names of distinct rites. || MJaiNyC_1,4.8-12 ||

In '<s>agnihotraṃ juhoti</s>' (one offers the <s>Agnihotra</s>) and '<s>āghāram āghārayati</s>' (one pours the <s>āghāra</s>), if the word '<s>agnihotra</s>' were a ritual name, then in the absence of [information about] the substance and deity, the very form of the sacrifice would not be established. Therefore, by this [word], the qualifying attribute of <s>Agni</s> as the deity is enjoined for the <s>darvihoma</s> (ladle-oblation). And the word '<s>āghāra</s>,' derived from the root '<s>ghṛ</s>' meaning 'to flow' or 'to shine,' denotes flowing ghee. Through the accusative case applied to that ghee, the status of being the object of preparatory rite (<s>saṃskārya</s>) is understood. And that prepared ghee becomes the substance for the <s>upāṃśuyāja</s> (silent offering). Therefore, the words '<s>agnihotra</s>' and '<s>āghāra</s>' enjoin a qualifying attribute and a preparatory rite, respectively — having arrived at this position, we say: Since the deity is already obtained through the <s>mantra</s> prescribed as '<s>agnir jyotiḥ, jyotir agniḥ svāhā</s>' (Agni is light, light is Agni, hail!) for the evening offering and '<s>sūryo jyotiḥ, jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā</s>' (Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, hail!) for the morning offering, the deity need not be [separately] enjoined. Therefore, for the rite whose deity is <s>Agni</s> or <s>Sūrya</s> and which is to be performed with restriction at the evening and morning times, '<s>agnihotra</s>' is an etymological name. The etymology is shown through the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound [= 'that in which the oblation to <s>Agni</s> is present']. Since the ghee-substance is already obtained by the passage '<s>caturgṛhītaṃ vā etad abhūt, tasyāghāram āghāryaḥ</s>' (that [offering] indeed became the four-fold grasped [ghee]; its pouring is the <s>āghāra</s>), and therefore the preparatory rite of flowing ghee need not be enjoined, the word '<s>āghāra</s>' too is an etymological name of the rite — [namely] that rite in which, from the southwestern direction to the northeastern direction, ghee is poured in a continuous stream, bears this name. Now, if these are names, then as in '<s>udbhidā yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Udbhid</s>) and '<s>jyotiṣṭomena yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice with the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>), for co-referentiality with the instrument denoted by the verbal root, the instrumental case should be used — [i.e.,] '<s>agnihotreṇa juhoti</s>' and '<s>āghāreṇāghārayati</s>.' This is not a fault.

children.translated_text: Therefore, the qualifying attribute of the simile, the bird, exists in the thing compared, the sacrifice — hence the word '<s>śyena</s>' is a name of the black-magic sacrifice.
'<s>Saṃdaṃśena abhicaran yajeta</s>' (one who performs black magic should sacrifice with the <s>Saṃdaṃśa</s>).

In '<s>gavā abhicaryamāṇo yajeta</s>' (one who is being attacked by black magic should sacrifice with the <s>Gava</s>), the name-status of the words <s>saṃdaṃśa</s> and <s>go</s> should be understood in the same way as the word '<s>śyena</s>'.

children.text: "yathā saṃdaṃśena durādānamādatte" "yathā gāvo gopāyanti"iti vākyaśeṣābhyāmupamānopameyabhāvābhidhānāt || MJaiNyC_1,4.13-15 ||
children.translated_text: Because the relation of simile and thing compared is stated through the complementary passages: '<s>yathā saṃdaṃśena durādānam ādatte</s>' (just as one takes something hard to reach with tongs) and '<s>yathā gāvo gopāyanti</s>' (just as cows protect). || MJaiNyC_1,4.13-15 ||

In '<s>śyenenābhicaran yajeta</s>' (one who performs black magic should sacrifice with the <s>Śyena</s>), if [the word '<s>śyena</s>'] were a name of the sacrifice, then since there would be no substance (<s>dravya</s>) or deity (<s>devatā</s>), even the essential nature of the sacrifice would not be established. Therefore, overriding the <s>Soma</s> substance that is permanently [required] in the <s>Soma</s> sacrifice, a desiderative qualifying attribute in the form of a bird-substance is enjoined. This being so, the conventional meaning (<s>rūḍhi</s>) of the word '<s>śyena</s>' as denoting a bird is supported. Nor can a splitting of the sentence be brought about as in the case of the <s>Citrā</s> sacrifice, when it is treated as a qualifying-attribute injunction — because the two qualifying attributes of variegatedness and femininity, [which were present] in the <s>Citrā</s> case, are absent here — having arrived at this position, we say: The relation of simile and thing compared stated in the passage '<s>yathā vai śyeno nipatyādatte, evam ayaṃ dviṣantaṃ bhrātṛvyaṃ nipatyādatte yam abhicarati śyenena</s>' (just as a hawk, swooping down, seizes [its prey], so does this [sacrificer] swoop down upon and seize the hostile rival whom he attacks with the <s>Śyena</s>) cannot apply to a single entity, the bird.

children.translated_text: because there would be the absurd consequence of splitting the sentence.
'One should perform the sacrifice with the substance' — this is one sentence.
'One should produce the fruit through the sacrifice' — this is another.

children.text: tasmādvājapeyaśabdo na guṇavidhāyakaḥ, kintu yathektaṃ dravyaṃ nimittīkṛtyāgnihotraśabdavatkarmanāmadheyam || MJaiNyC_1,4.15*-18 ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, the word '<s>Vājapeya</s>' is not an injunction of a qualifying attribute, but rather, like the word '<s>Agnihotra</s>,' it is a name of the sacrifice, based on a particular substance as its occasion. || MJaiNyC_1,4.15*-18 ||

In '<s>vājapeyena svārājyakāmo yajeta</s>' (one who desires sovereignty should sacrifice with the <s>Vājapeya</s>), by the word '<s>Vājapeya</s>' a qualifying attribute is enjoined. The word '<s>vāja</s>' means food. And that food which is to be drunk (<s>peya</s>) is the <s>surā</s> (liquor) substance. And that is the qualifying attribute here, because <s>surā</s>-vessels are to be employed [in the sacrifice]. Now, if it be objected that in treating it as a qualifying attribute, a secondary usage of the possessive type (<s>matvarthalakṣaṇā</s>) would follow — 'one should produce sovereignty through a sacrifice possessing the qualifying attribute <s>Vājapeya</s>' — not so. Because the verb '<s>yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice), uttered once, is accepted as connected by <s>tantra</s> (single operation) with both the qualifying attribute '<s>Vājapeya</s>' and the fruit 'sovereignty.' 'One should sacrifice with the substance <s>Vājapeya</s> for the sake of sovereignty' — thus both connections [are established]. Now, if it be objected: when connected with the qualifying attribute, the verb '<s>yaj</s>' takes the form 'one should perform the sacrifice with the qualifying attribute <s>Vājapeya</s>' — thus it has the role of object (<s>karmakaraka</s>); but when connected with the fruit, [it takes the form] 'one should accomplish sovereignty through the sacrifice' — thus it has the role of instrument (<s>karaṇakāraka</s>). How then can both connections hold simultaneously? This is not a defect. Because, due to the general nature of the verb '<s>yaj</s>,' a dual form is possible. In '<s>yajeta</s>' (one should sacrifice), the root expresses the sacrifice, the suffix expresses the productive force (<s>bhāvanā</s>), and from their combination only a connection in general is understood — and that [connection] is common to both the object-role and the instrument-role. Indeed, no specific, unambiguous case-ending that directly denotes either the object-role or the instrument-role is heard there. Therefore, when the general verb '<s>yaj</s>' is simultaneously connected with both, the specific type of connection is determined as appropriate. Thus, when connection through <s>tantra</s> is accepted, since the meaning 'one should perform the sacrifice with the <s>Vājapeya</s> substance' is obtained, even when treating it as a qualifying-attribute injunction, there is no possessive secondary usage. If the same qualifying-attribute analysis were applied to <s>Udbhid</s> and similar [sacrifices] as well, then those sentences too should be cited here and their established conclusion should be challenged again — having arrived at this position, we say: When the verb '<s>yaj</s>' is connected through <s>tantra</s> with both [the qualifying attribute and the fruit], the absurd consequence of a conflicting pair of triads would arise. The first triad consists of: being adoptable (<s>upādeyatva</s>), being enjoined (<s>vidheyatva</s>), and being a qualifying attribute (<s>guṇatva</s>). The second triad consists of: being the intended goal (<s>uddeśyatva</s>), being re-stated (<s>anuvādyatva</s>), and being primary (<s>mukhyatva</s>). Among these, the three — being the intended goal and so on — are properties belonging to the fruit of sovereignty. The three — being adoptable and so on — are properties belonging to the verb '<s>yaj</s>' which is the means. The verb '<s>yaj</s>' is subordinate with reference to the fruit. The intended-goal status of the fruit means it has the character of being the object with reference to the cognitive desire. The adoptable status of the verb '<s>yaj</s>' means it has the character of being practiced. Both of these are properties conditioned by mind and body. But the properties of being re-stated and being enjoined are conditioned by words. Re-statement (<s>anuvāda</s>) is the mention of what is already known. Injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) is the declaration that what is unknown is to be practiced. The fruit and the sacrifice have the relationship of end and means, [hence] principality and subordination respectively. This being so, when we examine the intrinsic nature of the fruit and its means — sovereignty and sacrifice — just as the fruit has the triad of intended-goal status and so on, and the sacrifice has the triad of adoptable status and so on, similarly when we examine the end-means relationship between the sacrifice and the <s>Vājapeya</s> substance, the sacrifice acquires the triad of intended-goal status and so on, and the <s>Vājapeya</s> substance acquires the triad of adoptable status and so on. Thus, when the sacrifice is simultaneously connected with both the fruit and the substance, the conflicting pair of triads ensues. Now, if it be said: then let there not be simultaneous connection through <s>tantra</s>; let the verb '<s>yaj</s>' be repeated for separate connections —
START MJaiNy 1,4.19-20
(In the seventh <s>adhikaraṇa</s>, on the non-name-status of words like '<s>Āgneya</s>' and the like, the <s>sūtra</s> is:)

children.text: tadguṇās tu vidhāyer annavibhāgād vidhānārthe na ced anyena śiṣṭāḥ / Jaim_1,4.9 /
children.translated_text: But its qualifying attributes [are the subject of] injunction — due to the distinction of food-materials, [it is] for the purpose of injunction, if not already prescribed by another [text]. / Jaim_1,4.9 /
He composes the seventh <s>adhikaraṇa</s> —
In '<s>yadāgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ</s>' (the <s>Āgneya</s> eight-potsherded [offering]) — is [the word '<s>Āgneya</s>'] a name or a qualifying attribute?
It is a name, like '<s>Agnihotra</s>' — not so, because if it were a name, there would be no deity. // MJaiNy_1,4.19 //
Nor is there a directly enjoined <s>mantra</s> here [to supply the deity]; the <s>taddhita</s> suffix enjoins the deity;
since the injunction is of [the sacrifice] qualified by [both] deity and substance, there is unity of sentence (<s>ekavākyatā</s>). // MJaiNy_1,4.20 //

children.translated_text: Because the <s>taddhita</s> suffix is derived in the meaning '<s>Agni</s> is the deity of this [offering].'
Nor should it be objected that since two qualifying attributes — substance and deity — are both enjoined, there would be a splitting of the sentence.
